Inflated multinomial logit regression

Source: R/estimators.R
imnl.Rd

Fits the baseline-inflated multinomial logit of Bagozzi and Marchetti (2017) and its generalization to any inflated alternative: a mixture of a degenerate distribution at the inflated alternative \(k\) and the multinomial / conditional logit of mnl(), with a binary split equation deciding which regime a case is in. The canonical application is vote choice with abstention as the base: routine nonvoters (the captive regime, always abstain) are mixed with occasional nonvoters and voters (the choice regime, the multinomial process), and the split equation separates them.

Usage

imnl(
  formula,
  data,
  inflate = NULL,
  id = NULL,
  alt = NULL,
  ref = NULL,
  link = c("logit", "probit"),
  weights = NULL,
  offset = NULL,
  fe = NULL,
  se = c("analytic", "opg", "robust", "cluster", "bootstrap", "none"),
  cluster = NULL,
  nboot = 200L,
  cores = 1L,
  start = NULL,
  maxit = 1000L,
  reltol = 1e-10,
  crosscheck = FALSE
)

Arguments

formula

A formula; see the section "Two data layouts" of mnl().

data

A data frame.

inflate

The inflated alternative: a level of the response. Default: ref, the base alternative (baseline inflation). Several levels give the model with a captive share for each (see Details).

id, alt

For the long layout, the names of the case and alternative columns of data. Leave both NULL for the wide layout.

ref

The base (reference) alternative: a level of the response. Default: the first level.

link

Link of the split equation: "logit" (default; the published model) or "probit".

weights

Optional frequency weights: a column name in data or a numeric vector with one entry per row (constant within a case in the long layout).

offset

Optional offset on the utility scale: in the long layout a column name or a vector with one entry per row; in the wide layout an \(n \times J\) matrix (columns in level order).

fe

Not available for the inflated model (see Details); an error if given.

se

Standard errors: "analytic" (inverse observed information, default), "opg", "robust", "cluster" (needs cluster), "bootstrap" (nonparametric over cases, or over clusters when cluster is given, with nboot refits from the full-sample estimate), or "none".

cluster

Optional cluster identifier (a column name in data or a vector aligned to its rows, constant within a case); supplying it selects se = "cluster" unless se is given explicitly.

nboot

Number of bootstrap refits for se = "bootstrap" (default 200).

cores

Number of parallel workers for the bootstrap (a PSOCK cluster; default 1). set.seed() before the call makes the resamples reproducible; serial and parallel runs use different random streams.

start

Optional starting values, which replace the multistart: the full parameter vector in the order of coef(), the outcome coefficients and then the split coefficients (infl_), on the same scale as coef() (object$theta of an earlier fit).

maxit, reltol

Controls for the BFGS stage passed to stats::optim() (the plain mnl() is solved by damped Newton steps first, with BFGS as the fallback); the Newton polish that follows runs up to 25 further iterations with the analytic Hessian of the logit family or central differences of the analytic gradient otherwise.

crosscheck

With one inflated alternative, also search under the other split link and polish this link's fit from its rescaled estimates (see Details); about doubles the fitting time. FALSE (default) skips it. Ignored with several inflated alternatives (which take the logit link only) and when start is given. The parametric-bootstrap refits of boot_lr_test() and boot_pvalue() search as the fit did.

Value

An object of class c("imnl", "choicemodel"); as mnl() plus phi (the fitted \(P(s_i = 1)\)), prob_outcome (the \(n \times J\) outcome-stage probabilities \(P_{ij}\)), inflate, and link; with several inflated alternatives also regime, the matrix of the regime probabilities.

Details

With \(s_i \in \{0, 1\}\), \(P(s_i = 1 \mid z_i) = \phi_i = F(z_i'\delta)\) (\(F\) logistic by default, or standard normal), and the mnl() probabilities \(P_{ij}\), $$P(y_i = k) = (1 - \phi_i) + \phi_i P_{ik}, \qquad P(y_i = j) = \phi_i P_{ij}, \; j \ne k.$$ In the discrete-choice literature, a model with a logit split equation is the parametrized logit captivity model of Swait and Ben-Akiva (1987, eq. 3) with captivity to \(k\) only. That model generalizes the dogit of Gaudry and Dagenais (1979), which adds to the multinomial logit a share of decision makers captive to each alternative, by making the captivity odds \(\theta_{ik} = (1 - \phi_i)/\phi_i\) a function of covariates; here \(\theta_{ik} = e^{-z_i'\delta}\), so the split coefficients are the negatives of Swait and Ben-Akiva's captivity coefficients.

Several inflated alternatives (inflate = c("abstain", "A")) give the parametrized logit captivity model with captive shares for each of them (Swait and Ben-Akiva 1987), which suits, say, routine nonvoters together with partisans captive to their party. The regimes (choosing, or captive to one of the inflated alternatives \(c \in C\)) follow a multinomial logit in \(z\): with \(\eta_{ic} = z_i'\delta_c\), $$\pi_{i0} = \frac{1}{1 + \sum_{c} e^{-\eta_{ic}}}, \qquad \pi_{ic} = \frac{e^{-\eta_{ic}}}{1 + \sum_{c} e^{-\eta_{ic}}}, \qquad P(y_i = j) = \pi_{i0} P_{ij} + 1\{j \in C\}\, \pi_{ij},$$ so \(\eta_{ic}\) is the log-odds of choosing against captivity to \(c\): a positive coefficient makes captivity to \(c\) less likely, the reading of the single split equation, which is the case \(|C| = 1\). Every inflated alternative gets its own coefficients on the same \(z\) (named infl_<alternative>:<term>; Swait and Ben-Akiva allow each alternative its own captivity covariates, while here every inflated alternative's equation has the same \(z\)); an inflated alternative outside a case's choice set is not one of its regimes. Several inflated alternatives take the logit split only. predict(type = "regime") then returns the matrix of the regime probabilities and type = "posterior" their posteriors given the observed choice; phi is the probability of the choice regime. A captive share that collapses to zero for every case is flagged boundary; the model with fewer inflated alternatives is nested at that boundary, so boot_lr_test() compares the two (as it compares the inflated model with mnl()). Each captive share is identified mainly through the mixture's form, as the single one is; an exclusion restriction helps. In the package's simulation (four alternatives, two of them captive, 200 samples per design), with a split covariate outside the outcome equations the 95 percent intervals covered 0.92-0.975 at n = 5,000; at n = 2,000 two cells missed, the constant of c's split equation (coverage 0.915) and its slope (a bias of -3.1 Monte Carlo standard errors). With the split on an outcome covariate instead, 3 of 200 fits at n = 5,000 had diverging choice coefficients (flagged boundary) and the intervals of that covariate's outcome coefficients covered 0.89-0.90; at n = 2,000, 17 of 200 fits were at a boundary and those intervals covered 0.80-0.81.

The MNL is the boundary case \(\phi \to 1\), where the split coefficients are not identified, so neither the chi-square reference of a likelihood-ratio test nor the normal reference of vuong() holds for the comparison with mnl(): boot_lr_test() calibrates both statistics by a parametric bootstrap under the MNL (the information criteria are a descriptive complement). The exception is a single inflated alternative with an intercept-only split (y ~ x | 1, a constant captive share), whose comparison with the MNL has a regular boundary: lr_test() and captivity_test(type = "lr") refer it to the 50:50 chi-square mixture. The split-equation coefficients are reported with the prefix infl_. Identification rests on the mixture structure, as for the zero-inflated count and inflated ordered models: an exclusion restriction (a variable in z not in x, or vice versa) is advisable but not required (Bagozzi and Marchetti 2017). The split equation models \(P(s_i = 1)\), the probability of being in the CHOICE regime: a positive coefficient means the covariate makes a case less likely to be a routine chooser of the inflated alternative. predict(type = "regime") returns \(\phi_i\) (and 1 for a case whose choice set lacks \(k\): the captive regime is impossible there, so such cases count as in the choice regime; the boundary check and summary()'s mean of \(\phi_i\) leave them out), type = "posterior" the regime probability given the observed choice (\(\phi_i P_{ik} / P^*_{ik}\) for a case that chose \(k\), 1 otherwise), which classifies the observed choosers of \(k\) into routine and occasional ones.

The formula has the split equation as its last part: in the wide layout y ~ x1 + x2 | z1 + z2, in the long layout choice ~ w1 | x1 + x2 | z1 + z2 (write | 1 | for an empty case-specific part). Everything else – layouts, weights, offsets, standard errors – is as in mnl(). Unit fixed effects are not available: with a constant per unit in the outcome equations the level of \(\phi\) is identified only through the functional form of the mixture, units that always chose the inflated alternative (the routine choosers the model is designed for) drop out, units with few such choices have them all put in the captive regime and their constants run to infinity, and units that never chose it pull \(\phi\) towards 1. In the package's simulations the split coefficients came out 25 to 42 percent too large at 12 to 20 cases per unit (and two to three times too large at 4), with a third or more of the unit constants at infinity, so imnl() refuses fe; for panels, fit without it with cluster set to the unit, or use mnl() with fe for the outcome equations.

The inflated likelihood can have several local maxima (it has two on each of pa2006 and pres2004, and many where the split equation can separate a few cases into the inflated regime). Estimation therefore runs a grid of fourteen starts (the mnl() coefficients, or an MNL that down-weights the inflated-alternative cases, combined with a binary fit of \(1\{y \ne k\}\) on \(z\) at full, halved, doubled, tripled, or zero slopes and several shifts of the split intercept), screens them by quasi-Newton, and polishes every screened start to convergence with the analytic Hessian. The incumbent is then challenged with its split slopes halved, enlarged by half, and doubled, again from each new incumbent (at most three rounds). With one inflated alternative, crosscheck = TRUE adds before the challengers the same search under the other split link, whose estimates, the split coefficients rescaled by 1.6 (the ratio of the logistic and normal densities at zero), are polished under this link as one more candidate: the two links' surfaces differ, and on the vote-choice data of Glasgow (2001) the logit split's own search ends 4.9 log-likelihood units below the maximum it reaches from the probit split's estimates. It about doubles the fitting time, so it is not the default; use it when the message reports several maxima. The highest maximum found is reported; it need not be the global one, so probe other basins with start too. The challengers start from the best polished fit only, so where the split coefficients diverge (the likelihood then has many flat plateaus, each a different hard classification of a few cases into the regimes) the plateau reported depends on the search path; such a fit is flagged boundary, and its split estimates are not maxima to interpret. The log-likelihoods of the polished starts (converged or not), of the cross-check and of the challengers that converged or improved, and the maximum reached by a saddle step, are in object$start_logliks, those of all screened starts in object$screen_logliks, the distinct points where these searches ended, each classified as a local maximum, a boundary (diverging coefficients or a split equation at one regime), a saddle, or not converged, in object$search (with their estimates in object$search_theta), the number of distinct local maxima among them in object$n_modes (see the section "Fit-quality flags" of mnl()), and with crosscheck = TRUE the cross-check in object$crosscheck (the other link's maximum, the maximum this link reached from it, and whether that improved on this link's own search); a message reports multimodality. A fit whose split equation puts every case in one regime has collapsed onto the MNL; it is flagged boundary with a warning.

The likelihood can also rise without bound along a direction of the outcome coefficients, to a supremum at infinity: separation within the mixture. The outcome stage can then predict some cases of the inflated alternative with certainty while the split equation puts its other cases in the captive regime, which overlapping data under the multinomial logit do not prevent (separation() checks the multinomial logit and the rank-ordered logit only). Strictly, the maximum-likelihood estimate then does not exist, and the reported fit is the highest end the search reaches. On pres2004 a search from 200 starts finds two interior maxima, the published fit (-545.279) and -550.259, and from two starts points where the Kerry and Bush coefficients diverge together, the higher at -542.851: 21 abstainers are predicted with certainty by the outcome stage and the other 84 are captive. The multistart does not reach that region; a fit started there is flagged (diverging coefficients, boundary, a singular information matrix). On pa2006 the same search finds the multistart's two maxima (-2069.971 and -2070.990) and no higher point.

References

Bagozzi, B.E. and Marchetti, K. (2017). Distinguishing occasional abstention from routine indifference in models of vote choice. Political Science Research and Methods, 5(2), 277-294. doi:10.1017/psrm.2015.42

Gaudry, M.J.I. and Dagenais, M.G. (1979). The dogit model. Transportation Research Part B, 13, 105-111. doi:10.1016/0191-2615(79)90028-6

Swait, J. and Ben-Akiva, M. (1987). Empirical test of a constrained choice discrete model: mode choice in Sao Paulo, Brazil. Transportation Research Part B, 21, 103-115. doi:10.1016/0191-2615(87)90010-5

mnl(), predict.choicemodel(), first_difference(), vuong()

Examples

set.seed(2)
d <- rmnl(800, beta = cbind(b = c(0.5, -1, 0.8), c = c(-0.3, 0.6, -0.5)),
          delta = c(0.5, 1.2), inflate = "a")
m <- imnl(y ~ x1 + x2 | z1, data = d, inflate = "a")
summary(m)
#> Inflated multinomial logit (inflated alternative: a, logit split) 
#> Call: imnl(formula = y ~ x1 + x2 | z1, data = d, inflate = "a")
#> Alternatives: a, b, c  (base: a)
#> 
#> Outcome equations (alternative:term):
#>               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> b:(Intercept)   0.1103     0.2484   0.444 0.657001    
#> b:x1           -0.9214     0.1858  -4.959 7.10e-07 ***
#> b:x2            0.8229     0.1575   5.224 1.75e-07 ***
#> c:(Intercept)  -0.8921     0.2630  -3.392 0.000693 ***
#> c:x1            0.7548     0.1765   4.277 1.90e-05 ***
#> c:x2           -0.5546     0.1701  -3.259 0.001117 ** 
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#> Split equation (P(choice regime) = F(z'delta)):
#>                  Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> infl_(Intercept)   0.7931     0.3404   2.330   0.0198 *  
#> infl_z1            1.4749     0.2994   4.927 8.37e-07 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#> Standard errors: analytic. Log-likelihood -625.233 on 8 parameters, 800 cases. AIC 1266.47, BIC 1303.94.
#> Inflated alternative 'a': observed share 0.559; mean fitted P(choice regime) 0.660.
## the inflated model nests the multinomial logit at a boundary (phi = 1): compare the
## two by information criteria here, or by boot_lr_test(m0, m)
m0 <- mnl(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d)
compare_models(m0, m)
